It suspends county permit, plan-review, and inspection approvals for BESS and data center construction in unincorporated areas until a 'Comprehensive Health and Safety Review' (covering fire/life-safety, cybersecurity/foreign-adversary equipment verification tied to the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act and the Governor's Prohibited Technologies List, and an Energy Development Zone siting study) is complete, with the Commissioners Court retaining sole discretion over when that review is finished. It requires County Fire Marshal plan review/approval and an independent third-party engineering evaluation before construction, and authorizes the County's legal counsel to seek injunctive relief against violators.
moratoria.trigger_text: Comprehensive health and safety review of AI data centers and battery energy storage systems
moratoria.current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The Commissioners Court unanimously adopted the signed order on 2026-07-27 following the July 13, 2026 public hearing; KWHI (2026-07-28) independently confirms the unanimous vote and describes the order's scope (equipment-manufacturer audits, an Energy Development Zone siting study by the County Fire Marshal and County Engineer, and injunctive-relief enforcement authority). No fixed term applies; the order remains in effect, by its own terms, until the Commissioners Court (in consultation with the County Fire Marshal) determines the Comprehensive Health and Safety Review is complete. No repeal, rescission, or completion of the review was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23. KWHI notes Austin County is 'the second county in Texas to adopt a moratorium of this nature,' after Hill County (which later rescinded its moratorium following a developer lawsuit; see the existing tx-hill-county-2026 row).

moratoria.duration: 180-day emergency water protection review period, through 2026-12-31 per tracker
moratoria.legal_basis: Hays County Commissioners Court resolution creating an 'emergency water protection review period'
moratoria.trigger_text: Water crisis / groundwater resource concerns from rapid data center growth
moratoria.current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; Commissioners Court adopted a resolution on 2026-06-23 creating an emergency water-protection review period that pauses approvals for data centers and other high-water-use developments, and creates a review task force. County officials and an attorney for Save Our Springs Alliance both stressed the resolution is deliberately not styled a 'moratorium' (to reduce litigation risk after Hill County's moratorium was rescinded and sued over), even though it functions as a development pause. [VERIFY instrument number; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.6 in the 2026-09 refresh]

moratoria.duration: Initial 120 days from 2026-05-20; City Attorney Mark Sossi described the subsequent 60-day extension (first reading reported ~2026-08-13, second/final reading ~2 weeks later) as 'the maximum extension allowed by law,' bringing the total pause to 180 days. Multiple August 2026 reports describe the extended pause as running 'through December' 2026.
moratoria.trigger_text: Precautionary study of potential future data center impacts and modernization of land use regulations; one source (Rio Grande Guardian) noted no data center projects were formally proposed within city limits at the time
moratoria.current_status: Active/extended as of 2026-09-23. Before the original 120-day term lapsed, the City Commission gave first reading to a 60-day extension ordinance (reported by KRGV on 2026-08-25 as approved 'last week') and a second/final reading roughly two weeks later, extending the moratorium to the 180-day statutory maximum (through approximately December 2026) while a contracted engineering firm (Ambiotec Engineering) completes a water/wastewater/electrical infrastructure impact study. The moratorium has no effect on the Fluidstack- and Eneus Energy-linked data center projects proposed just outside city limits near the Port of Harlingen/Valley International Airport, since those sites are in unincorporated Cameron County, outside the city's zoning jurisdiction (per Mayor Norma Sepulveda, 2026-09). No numbered city ordinance ('Ordinance No. ___') for either the original moratorium or the extension was located on harlingentx.gov or in news coverage reviewed, so the instrument-number portion of the original VERIFY marker remains open.

moratoria.duration: One year (as adopted; rescinded before completing its term)
moratoria.trigger_text: Development pressure from multiple (reportedly up to eight) proposed data center projects in a rural North Texas county
moratoria.current_status: Rescinded. Following a $100 million federal lawsuit filed by a data center developer (~2026-05-28) alleging the moratorium was illegal, the Hill County Commissioners Court voted to rescind the moratorium on 2026-06-04 and adopted new data center review requirements/policies instead (per KWTX, KCENTV, KXXV, and The Texas Tribune). The developer subsequently dismissed the lawsuit (KWTX, 2026-07-15) after the county's about-face and a settlement of up to $100,000.

moratoria.current_status: Expired. Per the eticaag BESS tracker, League City's pause on battery storage projects ran 2024-03-01 to 2024-07-01 (about 3 months) and has since lifted; the city went on to adopt a BESS ordinance (Chapter 125 of the Code of Ordinances). moratoria.current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23 per the eticaag BESS tracker (expiring October 2026); City Council has held at least one public hearing (2025-01-06) on extending its moratorium on issuance of permits for placement/installation of BESS facilities. [VERIFY instrument number not confirmed at confidence 0.6 in the 2026-09 refresh]

moratoria.duration: Proposed 90 days, with a possible optional 90-day extension (would push consideration of a large-scale data center to June 2027 if extended); an 18-month moratorium originally proposed by the citizen 'Save Lubbock' group was deemed not feasible under Texas law.
moratoria.legal_basis: City Council resolution (2026-09-23) initiating the process toward a data center moratorium ordinance, prompted by a citizen petition from the 'Save Lubbock' group; not yet a moratorium ordinance itself.
moratoria.trigger_text: regulatory_gap and specific_project concerns, driven by a citizen petition ('Save Lubbock' group led by Stephen Sanders); Council members cited ERCOT grid conditions and a desire to await further state-level guidance/regulation before large-scale data center development proceeds.
moratoria.current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23 (adopted same day as this research date). The Council voted 5-2 to adopt a resolution starting the moratorium process; while the ordinance is drafted, city planning staff are directed to develop guidelines on water use, power reliability, zoning, noise, and lighting for large-scale data centers, and a work session for the Council to be briefed on impacts is to be scheduled within 90 days. No moratorium ordinance has yet been adopted; per Mayor Mark McBrayer, the near-term practical effect is limited since 'no one's coming to Lubbock in the next year anyway with a data center' given current ERCOT conditions. [VERIFY instrument number; adoption date; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.6 in the 2026-09 refresh]

moratoria.duration: Proposed 3 months (per Councilmember Suzi Rumohr's public statement)
moratoria.legal_basis: Not yet adopted; a proposed ordinance following a two-track process (moratorium plus separate development-code amendments) is pending Council hearings.
moratoria.trigger_text: grid_energy/infrastructure_capacity: Denton Municipal Electric's transmission system is reported to be operating near capacity, with roughly $300 million in proposed transmission upgrades awaiting an ERCOT response; residents also cited water and community-benefit concerns relative to the roughly $3.5 million in taxes and $9 million in electric ROI/franchise fees existing data centers generate.
moratoria.current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23. The Council held the first of two required public hearings on 2026-09-22, at which all 20 public speakers supported the moratorium (some wanting it stronger); no vote was taken. A second public hearing is scheduled for 2026-10-27, and city officials have outlined a process that could bring the proposal back for final Council consideration as early as 2026-12-02. If adopted, the proposed moratorium would temporarily halt the city's acceptance, processing, and approval of new data center development applications (not affecting already-approved projects). [VERIFY instrument number; adoption date; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.6 in the 2026-09 refresh]

moratoria.duration: Proposed 90 days, extendable once by an additional 90 days (to a 180-day maximum); per the city's own timeline as of August 2026, the moratorium itself would not take effect until approximately Feb. 16, 2027 (running to approximately May 17, 2027, extendable to Aug. 15, 2027), after which state law bars the city from imposing another moratorium for two years.
moratoria.legal_basis: City Council resolution (Aug. 11, 2026) initiating the statutory process toward a data center moratorium ordinance; not yet a moratorium ordinance itself.
moratoria.trigger_text: regulatory_gap and specific_project concerns: sustained public pushback over multiple proposed/under-construction data centers within city limits and the ETJ (e.g., a $10 billion project within 300 feet of a resident's historic garden), a Fort Worth Zoning Commission vote against recommending an initial package of data center zoning regulations (July 2026) as rushed, and a directive from five Council members calling for a moratorium.
moratoria.current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23. Fort Worth has not yet adopted a data center moratorium; the Aug. 11, 2026 Council action only began the required legal process (two public hearings plus a two-reading ordinance vote) and created the advisory Data Center & Infrastructure Commission, whose recommendations are due at the council's Nov. 3, 2026 work session. Multiple September 2026 sources (Fort Worth Report, TCU 360, BenbrookLife.com) confirm the moratorium 'is not in place yet.' If the Council ultimately approves it by supermajority following the remaining hearings, city staff's own August 2026 timeline projected the pause would run from approximately Feb. 16, 2027 to May 17, 2027 (extendable to Aug. 15, 2027). [VERIFY instrument number; adoption date; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.65 in the 2026-09 refresh]

moratoria.trigger_text: No existing UDC regulations addressing high-intensity data processing facilities
moratoria.current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23; the City Commission voted on 2026-09-01 (Resolution No. 2026-121) to direct the city manager to begin the formal process for a 90-day moratorium on high-intensity data processing facilities, private gaming clubs, quick-lube facilities, event centers and self-storage facilities. Under Texas law the moratorium requires three public hearings (30 days between the first and second) before it takes effect, so it had not yet taken effect as of the reference date.
